summary:
Zimbabwe criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. The offence covers sodomy and, per the Human Dignity Trust country profile, acts involving contact between males that would be regarded by a reasonable person as indecent, so conduct short of intercourse can still fall within the criminal law.

Amnesty International's report of 9 January 2024 (index AFR 01/7533/2024), 'We are facing extinction — escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponisation of law and their human rights implications in select African countries', examines rising anti-LGBTI sentiment and the use of law against LGBTI people in the countries it covers, Zimbabwe among them. The report's finding of law being deployed as an instrument of hostility is the operative risk context for a visitor, alongside the statutory exposure itself.

Healthcare access is formally protected. In July 2018 the Zimbabwean health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gay people, sex workers and transgender or non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states that care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty, recording that nowhere in policy or law states it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups. It was issued because patients had avoided clinics fearing mistreatment or police tip-offs by staff. For a trans visitor this means formal policy guarantees health-service access, including transition-relevant care at public facilities, though day-to-day treatment depends on staff trained under a 2018 handbook.

GALZ (Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe), a voluntary membership organisation established in 1990 with more than 4,000 community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups and 4 resource centres, provides legal support explicitly covering arrests for 'sodomy', counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes for LGBTI Zimbabweans. Legal aid and counselling remain reachable for an LGBTI traveller despite criminalisation.
tangentialFactors:
Social-science literature documents the social climate a visitor will enter. Mabvurira et al. (International Journal of Humanities and Social Science, July 2012) report that homosexual Zimbabweans live secluded lives because of prejudice, and argue that homosexuality is 'as African as the baobab tree and as Zimbabwean as the Great Zimbabwe Ruins', tracing same-sex relations in pre-colonial and post-colonial Zimbabwe; the authors call on social workers to promote social justice for the gay community. An article in the Journal of Homosexuality (Taylor & Francis) also examines homosexuality in Zimbabwe.

The Amnesty International report of 9 January 2024 situates Zimbabwe within a wider African pattern of escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law, so hostility a visitor encounters is not isolated to Zimbabwe alone.
localsOnly:
GALZ, established 1990, organises 10 affinity groups and operates 4 resource centres alongside its legal, counselling and hospital-fee assistance services for LGBTI Zimbabweans, with 35 years of advocacy behind it.

The 2018 health ministry handbook binds all health practitioners in public health institutions to serve key population groups, and its stated rationale was that patients had stayed away from clinics over fears of mistreatment or of staff tipping off police.

Social workers are urged in the academic literature to act for the gay community, and same-sex relations are documented in Zimbabwe's pre-colonial and post-colonial history.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether the 2018 handbook remains the operative health-sector instruction, whether it has been revised, withdrawn or reissued under a later administration, or how widely its training has actually been delivered since.

No source here states the statutory penalty for the sodomy or indecent-contact offences, nor whether any prosecution has been brought in recent years; the Human Dignity Trust profile is cited only for the scope of the offence.

Whether GALZ's four resource centres and legal support are accessible to a foreign national rather than to residents is not stated in the inventory.

Entry, visa and document-marker rules for trans travellers to Zimbabwe are not covered by any source supplied.
